blocks.x: Uganda is divided into **districts** for easier administration. Each district is divided into counties, sub-counties, parishes and villages. Uganda has **over 140 districts**, and the number **keeps changing** as new districts are created, so always use the number your teacher gives for the current year. **Kampala** is the capital city and is administered by the **Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA)**.
The country is often grouped into four regions: **Central, Eastern, Northern and Western**.
**Compass:** An instrument used to find direction.
**A way to remember the cardinals clockwise:** **N**ever **E**at **S**limy **W**orms.
Uganda's neighbours
Uganda is **landlocked** — it has no coastline of its own, so it uses the ports of **Mombasa** (Kenya) and **Dar es Salaam** (Tanzania).
Definitions
**Lines of latitude:** Imaginary lines running from **west to east** on the globe, showing how far a place is north or south of the Equator.
**Lines of longitude:** Imaginary lines running from the **North Pole to the South Pole**, showing how far a place is east or west of the Prime Meridian.
Uganda's position

items: Uganda lies between about **4°N and 1°S** of the Equator.
It lies between about **29°E and 35°E** of the Prime Meridian.
**The Equator (0°) passes through Uganda**, near Kayabwe on the Kampala–Masaka road, so part of Uganda is in the Northern Hemisphere and part in the Southern Hemisphere.

blocks.x: **Important:** the **Equator** is the most important line of latitude, at **0°**; the **Prime (Greenwich) Meridian** is the most important line of longitude, at **0°**.

Scale and grid reference
**Scale:** For example, *1 : 50,000* means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm (½ km) on the ground. So 6 cm on such a map = 3 km on the ground.
**Grid reference:** The numbered lines on a map. Read the **eastings (across) first**, then the **northings (up)** — "along the corridor, then up the stairs".

sections.title: 5. THE SIZE AND POSITION OF UGANDA

items: Uganda covers about **241,000 square kilometres** (about 241,550 km² including its open water and swamps).
About **one fifth** of the country is water and swamp — Lake Victoria alone is huge.
Uganda lies in **East Africa**, on the plateau between the two arms of the **Great Rift Valley**.
Its capital is **Kampala**; **Entebbe** has the international airport.
The **highest point** is Margherita Peak on Mt Rwenzori (5,109 m); the lowest area is the Albert Nile region.

**What you already know:** In P.4 you looked at the land forms in your district. In P.5 you name and locate the major physical features of the **whole of Uganda** and learn how they were formed.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

blocks.x: **Physical features:** The natural land forms found on the earth's surface.
They include **mountains, hills, plateaux, plains, rift valleys, lakes, rivers, waterfalls, swamps, islands and valleys**.
**Rift valley:** A deep and wide valley that stretches for a long distance, formed when land between two faults sinks.

sections.title: 3. THE RIFT VALLEY, PLATEAUX AND PLAINS

items: The **western arm of the Great Rift Valley** (the Albertine Rift) runs along Uganda's western border, holding **Lakes Albert, Edward and George** and the **Semliki** valley.
Most of Uganda is a **plateau** about 1,000–1,300 metres above sea level.
**Plains** and lowlands lie around Lake Kyoga and in the north.
**Depressions** and **valleys** are found between the hills.

blocks.x: **How lakes are formed:** by **faulting** (Albert, Edward, George), by **down-warping** (Victoria, Kyoga), by **volcanic action** (crater lakes such as Katwe), and by **people** building dams (man-made lakes).
Rivers

**The Nile** — the longest, leaving Lake Victoria at **Jinja** as the Victoria Nile, passing Lake Kyoga and Lake Albert, then flowing north as the **Albert Nile** · **Katonga** · **Kafu** · **Mpologoma** · **Aswa** · **Semliki** · **Sezibwa** · **Manafwa**.
Waterfalls
**Murchison (Kabalega) Falls** on the Victoria Nile · **Karuma Falls** · **Bujagali** and **Owen Falls** near Jinja · **Sipi Falls** on Mt Elgon · **Itanda Falls**.
Swamps and islands

Swamps lie around Lake Kyoga, Lake Victoria and along many rivers, and are important for water, papyrus and fish. Uganda's islands include the **Ssese Islands**, **Buvuma** and **Koome** in Lake Victoria.

sections.title: 5. HOW PHYSICAL FEATURES AFFECT PEOPLE'S LIVES

blocks.x: The good side

items: Mountains and highlands receive **relief rainfall** and have **fertile volcanic soils**, so farming is good.
Lakes and rivers give **water, fish, transport and hydro-electric power** (Nalubaale, Kiira, Bujagali, Isimba, Karuma).
Physical features attract **tourists** — the Rwenzori, Murchison Falls, the crater lakes, the source of the Nile.
Swamps supply **papyrus, clay and water** and control floods.
They form **natural boundaries** between districts and countries.

blocks.x: The difficult side

items: Mountains make **road building** hard and expensive.
Steep slopes cause **soil erosion and landslides**, as at Bududa on Mt Elgon.
Rivers and lakes **flood** and destroy crops and homes.
Swamps and lakes breed **mosquitoes and bilharzia snails**.
Some areas are cut off during the rains.

blocks.x: Caring for physical features

Plant trees on hills and river banks · dig **terraces and contour trenches** on slopes · do not build or farm in **swamps and wetlands** · avoid pouring waste into lakes and rivers · avoid **bush burning** and stone quarrying without restoring the land · obey the laws that protect wetlands, forests and lake shores.

**What you already know:** You know that some days are hot and others rainy. In P.5 you learn what **climate** is, the **climatic regions of Uganda**, what influences them, and how climate affects the way people live.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: explain the difference between weather and climate
identify and describe the major climatic regions of Uganda
explain the factors that influence the climate of Uganda
explain how climate influences human activities
identify problems associated with climate and suggest solutions

blocks.x: Definitions
**Weather:** The condition of the atmosphere of a place at a particular time.
**Climate:** The average weather conditions of a place recorded over a long period, usually 30 years or more.
Elements of weather and the instruments used
All these instruments are kept at a **weather station**, in a white wooden box called a **Stevenson screen**, which is painted white to reflect heat and has louvres to let air pass.
The syllabus groups Uganda's climate into **hot, wet and dry** regions. In more detail:

head: Region
Where
Characteristics
rows: Around Lake Victoria, the south-west and the Rwenzori foothills — Entebbe, Kampala, Masaka, Kalangala
Rain **almost all year**, over 1,200 mm; two rainy seasons (March–May and September–November); warm, 20–28 °C; high humidity
Most of central and northern Uganda — Lira, Gulu, Mbarara
A clear **wet season and dry season**; 750–1,200 mm of rain; hot by day
**Karamoja** and parts of Ankole and the rift valley floor
Under 750 mm of rain; long dry spells; very hot; unreliable rainfall
**Cool to cold**; heavy relief rainfall; snow on the Rwenzori peaks

sections.title: 3. FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE THE CLIMATE OF UGANDA

head: Factor
How it works
rows: The higher the place, the **cooler** it is — about 1 °C for every 150 m. This is why Kabale and the Rwenzori are cold and the rift valley floor is hot
Places near Lake Victoria get **more rainfall** and a moderate temperature
Mountains force air to rise, cool and give **relief rainfall** on the windward side; the leeward side stays dry (a **rain shadow**)
Forests give off water vapour, bringing more rain; when they are cut, rainfall reduces
Moist winds from the lakes and the Congo forest bring rain; dry winds from the north-east bring drought
Uganda lies on the **Equator**, so it is warm all year
Deforestation, swamp draining, bush burning and factory smoke change the climate

head: Region
Activities it favours
rows: Growing coffee, bananas, sugar cane, tea and vanilla; fishing; lumbering; dense settlement
Growing cotton, maize, millet, sorghum, groundnuts and simsim; cattle keeping; tourism in game parks
**Nomadic pastoralism**; growing drought-resistant crops such as sorghum and millet; bee keeping
Growing coffee, tea, bananas, Irish potatoes and vegetables on volcanic soils; tourism and lumbering

blocks.x: Climate also decides the **type of houses** people build, the **clothes** they wear, and even the **times** when they work in the gardens.

blocks.x: Climate change

Because of **deforestation, swamp draining, bush burning and smoke**, the rains in many parts of Uganda now come **late, stop early or fail**, while storms have become heavier. The cure is the same everywhere: **plant trees, protect wetlands and forests, and use energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar** instead of firewood and charcoal.

Reasons for migration

Search for **fertile land** and pasture · **population pressure** in the cradle land · **wars and internal conflicts** · **drought and famine** · **diseases and pests** · the wish to **expand and control new land** · following their **cattle**.
The routes and settlement

The **Bantu** came from the west and settled in the fertile, well-watered south and west. The **Luo** followed the **Nile valley** southwards from Bahr-el-Ghazal into Acholi, Lango and West Nile. The **Nilo-Hamites** moved south-west from the Ethiopian border into Karamoja and Teso. The **Hamites** came from the north-east into the western grasslands with their long-horned cattle.
Problems they met on the way

**Resistance** from people already living there · **wild animals** and **diseases** · **thick forests, rivers and swamps** · shortage of **food and water** · long distances on foot · language barriers.
Effects of the migrations

Population **increased** · new **skills** spread — iron working, farming and cattle keeping · **intermarriage** and new communities · **kingdoms and chiefdoms** were formed · but there were also **wars over land**, loss of land by earlier peoples, and the loss of some cultures.

items: People lived in **clans** made of related families, each with a **totem** (an animal or plant the clan does not eat or kill).
The **extended family** lived together and shared work and property.
**Marriage** was arranged between clans, with **bride price**; a person could not marry from their own clan.
**Traditional religion**: belief in a supreme god (**Katonda** in Buganda, **Ruhanga** in the west, **Jok** among the Luo), spirits and ancestors, with shrines and priests.
**Customs and ceremonies**: birth and twin ceremonies, naming, **initiation** (the *imbalu* circumcision of the Bagisu), marriage and burial rites.
Education was **informal** — children learnt by watching and helping, and through **folk tales, riddles, proverbs, songs and dances**.

blocks.x: How a centralised kingdom worked (Buganda as an example)

The **Kabaka** was the head, helped by the **Katikkiro** (prime minister), the **Lukiiko** (council), county chiefs (**Ssaza**), sub-county chiefs (**Ggombolola**) and parish chiefs (**Muluka**). The chiefs collected **tribute and taxes**, kept order, settled cases and raised an **army**. The Bachwezi and later the Babiito ruled the great western kingdoms.
How a decentralised society worked

The **clan elders** and the **rwot** or council of elders settled disputes, allocated land, led ceremonies and organised defence. Decisions were made by **discussion and agreement**, and there was no single king over all the people.
